title: Daily Pill (Oral PrEP)
tagline: A pill you take once a day to stay protected
keyTakeaways: Take one pill every day - you can do it at home on your own schedule
Over 99% effective at preventing HIV when taken daily as directed
Two medication options available: Truvada and Descovy
Most side effects are mild and usually go away within a few weeks
Easy to start and easy to stop - you're in control

sections.title: Overview
sections.content: Oral PrEP is the original form of PrEP and has been available since 2012. It's a single pill you take once a day to protect yourself from HIV. Because you take it at home, you have full control over your prevention - no clinic visits needed for each dose. Millions of people around the world use oral PrEP safely and successfully.
keyPoints: One pill, once a day
Take it at home - no injections needed
Available as a generic, which can lower costs
The longest track record of any PrEP option

sections.title: How It Works
sections.content: Oral PrEP contains two medications that work together to block HIV from making copies of itself in your body. When you take the pill daily, the medicine builds up in the tissues where HIV would try to enter - like the lining of the rectum and vaginal tissue. With enough medicine present, HIV can't get a foothold, even if you're exposed to the virus.
keyPoints: The two medicines block a key step HIV needs to reproduce
Protection builds up over the first several days of use
Consistent daily use keeps protective levels steady in your body

sections.title: Medications Available
sections.content: There are two brand-name medications approved for oral PrEP, and generic versions are also available. Both work very well, but they have some differences worth knowing about.
keyPoints: Truvada (tenofovir disoproxil fumarate + emtricitabine) - approved for all adults and adolescents at risk for HIV, regardless of the type of sex they have. Also available as a lower-cost generic.

Descovy (tenofovir alafenamide + emtricitabine) - approved for people at risk through sex, except it has not been studied in people at risk through receptive vaginal sex. May have fewer effects on kidneys and bones compared to Truvada.
Your provider can help you decide which one is the best choice for you based on your health and situation.

callouts.title: What about generics?
callouts.text: Generic versions of Truvada are available and work just as well as the brand-name version. Generics are often more affordable. Ask your provider or pharmacist about generic options.

sections.title: Dosing Schedule
sections.content: The standard approach is to take one pill every day, ideally around the same time each day. Many people find it helpful to tie it to a daily routine - like brushing your teeth, eating breakfast, or taking other vitamins. If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember. If it's almost time for your next dose, just take one pill - don't double up.
keyPoints: One pill, once a day, every day
Try to take it around the same time each day
If you miss a dose, take it as soon as you remember
Don't take two pills to make up for a missed dose

callouts.title: Tips for remembering
callouts.text: Set a daily alarm on your phone, use a pill organizer, or pair it with something you do every day like your morning coffee. Some people keep their PrEP next to their toothbrush as a visual reminder.

callouts.title: On-demand dosing (2-1-1)
callouts.text: For cisgender men who have sex with men, there is an alternative called on-demand or event-driven PrEP (sometimes called 2-1-1). This means taking 2 pills 2-24 hours before sex, then 1 pill 24 hours after the first dose, and 1 more pill 24 hours after that. This approach is not recommended for everyone - talk to your provider to see if it's an option for you.

sections.title: Effectiveness
sections.content: When taken every day as directed, oral PrEP reduces the risk of getting HIV from sex by more than 99%. That makes it one of the most effective prevention tools available. However, effectiveness depends on consistency - missing doses can lower your protection. Studies show that the more consistently you take it, the better it works.
keyPoints: More than 99% effective when taken daily
Even imperfect use still provides significant protection
Consistent use is key to maximum protection
Works for all types of sexual exposure when taken daily

callouts.title: Consistency matters
callouts.text: PrEP works best when you take it every day. If you find it hard to remember a daily pill, that's completely okay - it might mean one of the injectable options could be a better fit for you.

sections.title: Side Effects
sections.content: Most people tolerate oral PrEP very well. Some people experience mild side effects when they first start, but these usually go away within the first few weeks. Serious side effects are rare.
keyPoints: Common early side effects: mild nausea, headache, fatigue, or stomach upset
These 'start-up' side effects usually go away within 2-4 weeks
Truvada may affect kidney function or bone density in some people over time - your provider will monitor this with regular lab tests
Descovy generally has fewer effects on kidneys and bones
Serious side effects are uncommon

callouts.title: Managing early side effects
callouts.text: If you feel nauseous when you first start, try taking your pill with food or at bedtime. These feelings usually pass within a couple of weeks as your body adjusts.

sections.title: Getting Started
sections.content: Starting oral PrEP is straightforward. You'll need to see a healthcare provider who will make sure PrEP is right for you, run a few simple tests, and write you a prescription. Here's what to expect:
keyPoints: You'll get an HIV test to confirm you're HIV-negative before starting
Your provider will check your kidney function with a simple blood test
You may be tested for other STIs and hepatitis B
Once prescribed, you can pick up your medication at a pharmacy
Protection builds up over the first several days - about 7 days for receptive anal sex and about 21 days for receptive vaginal sex
Follow-up visits are typically every 3 months for HIV testing and check-ins

callouts.title: How quickly does it start working?
callouts.text: Oral PrEP reaches full protection for receptive anal sex after about 7 days of daily use. For receptive vaginal sex, it takes about 21 days. During this ramp-up period, use additional protection like condoms.

sections.title: Stopping Oral PrEP
sections.content: One of the advantages of oral PrEP is that it's easy to stop and restart. If your situation changes or you decide you no longer need PrEP, you can simply stop taking the pill. There's no complicated process involved.
keyPoints: You can stop taking oral PrEP at any time
Protection fades within a few days after stopping
If you might be exposed to HIV after stopping, use other protection like condoms
You can restart oral PrEP whenever you want - just see your provider for updated testing
Talk to your provider before stopping, especially if you have hepatitis B

callouts.title: Short tail period
callouts.text: Unlike injectable PrEP, oral PrEP leaves your system relatively quickly - within days after stopping. This means your protection fades fast, so be sure to use other prevention methods if you're still at risk.

sections.title: Cost & Access
sections.content: There are many programs to help make oral PrEP affordable - and for many people, it's available at no cost. Don't let worries about cost stop you from exploring PrEP.
keyPoints: Most insurance plans (including Medicaid) cover PrEP with no out-of-pocket cost
The Ready, Set, PrEP program provides free PrEP medication to people without prescription drug coverage
Gilead's Advancing Access program offers copay assistance for those with insurance
Generic versions of Truvada are available and typically cost less
Many clinics offer PrEP services on a sliding fee scale based on income

callouts.title: Don't have insurance?
callouts.text: The federal Ready, Set, PrEP program can provide PrEP medication at no cost if you don't have insurance that covers prescriptions. Visit your provider or a local health center to learn more about enrolling.

sections.title: Common Questions
sections.content: Here are answers to some of the questions people ask most often about oral PrEP.
keyPoints: Q: Will PrEP protect me from other STIs? - A: No, PrEP only prevents HIV. You can still use condoms and get tested regularly for other STIs.
Q: Can I drink alcohol while taking PrEP? - A: Yes. Alcohol does not affect how well PrEP works. However, be mindful that heavy drinking might make it harder to remember your daily pill.
Q: Will PrEP show up on a drug test? - A: No. PrEP will not show up on standard drug tests.

Q: Can I take PrEP if I'm pregnant or planning to become pregnant? - A: Truvada is considered safe during pregnancy and breastfeeding. Talk with your provider about the best choice for your situation.
Q: What if I want to switch to an injectable option later? - A: Absolutely! You can switch between PrEP options. Your provider will help you make a smooth transition.

Q: Do I still need to use condoms if I'm on PrEP? - A: PrEP is highly effective against HIV on its own. Condoms add extra protection against HIV and also protect against other STIs and pregnancy. It's your choice.
